newsitem.title: RWANDA: Canadian commander signals east Zaire visit.
newsitem.headline: Canadian commander signals east Zaire visit.

text.p: The Canadian commander of a proposed multinational force for eastern Zaire indicated on Wednesday that he might visit rebel-controlled eastern Zaire on Thursday in a bid to help establish who needed aid and where.
But Lieutenant-General Maurice Baril declined to say where outside the Rwandan capital of Kigali he would be going and said Rwanda's strongman saw little reason for a multinational force in Zaire.

"He sees little use for force on the ground because the situation is, according to him, fixing itself quite well even though he agrees there is a lot we don't know," Baril said after an hour of talks with Rwandan Vice-President Paul Kagame.

"He understands that ... as a commander, before I recommend that everything is fine I've got to be sure of what is the condition of those folks in the field. That he understands and he will cooperate with us as much as he can," Baril added.
The Rwandan government says any multinational force for Zaire is irrelevant as most Rwandan refugees have come home.
Officials have said it cannot use Rwandan territory for its operations following the return of an estimated 600,000 Rwandan refugees in five days starting on November 15.
"What we are trying to define precisely is what is the situation on the ground, how many folks and what condition they are in is what we are trying to find out," the general said.
He said he discussed with Kagame the results of weekend talks in Stuttgart between contributing states to the force and contingency plans in case of "a catastrophe somewhere".

Asked what was the situation on the ground in Zaire, Baril said: "That's what we are trying to find out and we're putting every means that we have -- very sophisticated right down to little old me, who is going to take a look at it tomorrow."
He declined to say where he would go on Thursday but said he would afterwards go to Entebbe, Uganda, to compare his information with "sensors" such as aerial surveillance from there.

Before seeing Kagame, Baril met the small Canadian military liaison team in Kigali and officers from Britain and the United States who have both been trying by aerial photographs to locate large masses of refugees in Zaire scattered by fighting.

Asked whether he had spoken to the Zairean rebels, Baril said that he had not but "I won't hesitate because the aim is to go and take care of the folks in the field...I will go and talk to whoever I have to and that is what I am going to do".
The Zairean rebels reject the multinational force for east Zaire, arguing there are few refugees in areas they control so any international military presence would prop up President Mobutu Sese Seko.
Baril said food airdrops would only be used if necessary.
"I would certainly like to have in my back pocket some sort of emergency tool, and parachuting or airdrop is one of the tools I would like to have. But it is not the best there is," he said.
He said he discussed airdrops with Kagame who assured him he would "use all his influence" to coordinate any air operation.

"Airdrop is...efficient because that's the way you have to go, but it is risky and not as efficient as a good old convoy on the road," said Baril, adding his mission's aim was to ensure aid agencies could do their job and he hoped they could soon.

"The problem with the multinational force is it was approved before the half a million refugees returned," said a diplomat in Kigali. "Now we have to find out where exactly the rest are, how many of them are there and what they need."
Uganda's foreign ministry said on Wednesday the government had agreed to the use of Entebbe airport as a base for international relief operations in the eastern Zaire crisis.
The Rwandan government says any aid would best be used within Rwandan territory, providing for the new returnees.
But aid agencies say a multinational force is needed to reach hundreds of thousands of Rwandan refugees and Zaireans displaced by the fighting outside rebel-held eastern Zaire.
Baril, 52, the commander of Canada's ground forces who was appointed to head the multinational humanitarian relief force on November 14, said he would fly back to Entebbe on Thursday.
